# Shear-warp
Also called: Shear-warp factorization

## Overview
The Shear-warp family solves the problem of efficient volume rendering from arbitrary viewing angles by factorizing the 3D viewing transformation into a 3D shear and a 2D warp [S1, unofficial][S12]. It sets itself apart from general ray-casting methods by transforming the volume into a "sheared object space" where viewing rays are parallel to a coordinate axis, allowing for efficient slice-by-slice compositing and fixed interpolation weights [S12]. Unlike [Splatting](23-splatting.md) or [Texture slicing](25-texture-slicing.md), it avoids the computational expense of per-ray traversal by leveraging spatial coherence and memory alignment through affine transformations [S3, S9, unofficial].

## Shared principles
The Shear-warp family shares the core mechanism of decomposing the viewing transformation matrix $M_{view}$ into three components: a permutation $P$, a shear $S$, and a 2D warp $M_{warp}$ [S2, unofficial][S12]. This factorization is expressed as:
$$ M_{view} = M_{warp} \cdot S \cdot P $$
The process generally involves two main phases: warping (resampling) and compositing [S1, unofficial].

1.  **Permutation (Axis Selection):** The algorithm determines the principal viewing axis by finding the coordinate axis (X, Y, or Z) most aligned with the view direction vector $v_o$ [S12]. A permutation matrix $P$ is constructed to align this axis with the Z-axis of an intermediate coordinate system [S2, unofficial][S12]. If the view is along X or Y, the voxel coordinates are reordered by transposing the axes [S3, unofficial]. To avoid re-encoding data when the view direction changes, three Run-Length Encoded (RLE) structures are typically pre-computed, one for each principal axis [S3, S17, unofficial].

2.  **Shear and Resampling:** The volume slices (perpendicular to the principal axis) are transformed into an intermediate 2D image space [S2, unofficial][S12]. The shear matrix $S$ transforms the volume such that viewing rays become parallel to the Z-axis [S2, unofficial]. For parallel projection, the shear coefficients $s_x, s_y$ are derived from the view direction $v_o = [v_{o,x}, v_{o,y}, v_{o,z}]^T$:
    $$ s_x = -\frac{v_{o,x}}{v_{o,z}}, \quad s_y = -\frac{v_{o,y}}{v_{o,z}} $$
    The shear matrix is:
    $$ S = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & s_x & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & s_y & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} $$
    Each slice is resampled into the intermediate image using bilinear interpolation [S2, unofficial][S12]. Because the shear ensures that sampling rays are perpendicular to the slices, fixed interpolation weights can be computed once per frame, exploiting spatial coherence [S3, S9, unofficial]. For perspective projection, an additional scaling factor is applied to each slice to account for foreshortening [S2, unofficial][S12].

3.  **Compositing:** The sheared slices are composited in front-to-back order into the intermediate image using the Porter-Duff "over" operator [S2, unofficial][S12]. This step projects the volume into a 2D intermediate image in sheared object space. Early ray termination is supported by skipping further slices for pixels where accumulated opacity exceeds a threshold (e.g., 0.95) [S2, unofficial][S11, abstract only, unofficial].

4.  **Warp:** The intermediate image is transformed to the final image space using the 2D warp matrix $M_{warp}$ [S2, unofficial][S12]. This step corrects the distortion introduced by the shear and applies the correct perspective/parallel projection [S22, unofficial]. The warp matrix is computed as:
    $$ M_{warp} = M_{view} \cdot S^{-1} \cdot P^{-1} $$
    (Note: Some sources define $M_{warp} = M_{view} \cdot M_{shear}^{-1}$ assuming $P$ is handled in the permutation step [S7, S21, unofficial]). The intermediate image is resampled using bilinear interpolation to produce the final image [S2, unofficial][S12].

## Subtopics

### [VolumePro Ray-Casting with Slice-by-Slice Processing](1865-volumepro-ray-casting-with-slice-by-slice-processing.md)
VolumePro is a specialized hardware architecture that implements object-space ray-casting with parallel slice-by-slice processing to achieve real-time frame rates on PC-class computers. It differs from texture-mapping approaches by supporting gradient estimation and per-sample Phong illumination in real-time, and from pre-processing approaches by allowing immediate visual feedback during parameter changes without lengthy recomputation. It builds on the Shear-warp method [24-shear-warp.md] by casting rays from the base plane (the volume face most parallel to the viewing plane) into the dataset, projecting the resulting base plane image onto the final image plane via a 3D transformation and 2D warping.

### [Affine-Transformations Method](2038-affine-transformations-method.md)
The Affine-Transformations Method is a hybrid volume rendering technique that uses affine transformations to warp volume slices or the entire volume into the image plane so that data samples become pixel-aligned, after which the transformed data is composited to calculate visibility. It is distinct from pure feed-backward (ray-casting) methods, which cast rays into the data set, and pure feed-forward (element-tossing) methods, which map data elements directly to the image plane. By aligning samples with pixels before compositing, it bridges the gap between these two extremes, leveraging the efficiency of feed-forward warping while maintaining the visibility handling of feed-backward approaches.

### [Shear-Warp Algorithm](4304-shear-warp-algorithm.md)
The Shear-Warp Algorithm is a fast, software-based volume rendering technique that reduces the number of resampling passes from three to two by factorizing the viewing transformation matrix into a 3D shear and a 2D warp. It solves the problem of efficient rendering from arbitrary viewing angles by transforming the volume data into a "sheared object space" where viewing rays are parallel to a coordinate axis, allowing for efficient slice-by-slice compositing. Unlike general ray-casting methods that perform trilinear interpolation per pixel, Shear-Warp substitutes this with fixed bilinear interpolation weights computed once per frame, exploiting spatial coherence and memory alignment. It is distinct from GPU-based ray marching by relying on CPU-driven affine transformations and intermediate image buffers, though it shares the slice-based processing logic with [Affine-Transformations Method](2038-affine-transformations-method.md).

### [Perspective Projection Rendering](5558-perspective-projection-rendering.md)
Perspective Projection Rendering is a volume rendering method that extends the shear-warp factorization to support perspective viewing transformations. It solves the problem of rendering volumetric data with correct perspective foreshortening, which parallel projection methods cannot handle natively. It sets itself apart from its siblings by scaling each volume slice during the resampling phase to account for distance from the camera, whereas [Shear-Warp Algorithm](4304-shear-warp-algorithm.md) and [Affine-Transformations Method](2038-affine-transformations-method.md) typically assume parallel projection or handle perspective differently.

### [Hybrid Shear-Warp and Polygon Rendering](5876-hybrid-shear-warp-and-polygon-rendering.md)
This method extends the Shear-warp algorithm to support the correct concurrent display of volume data and opaque polygonal geometry. It solves the problem of visual artifacts that arise when mixing ray-cast volumes with rasterized surfaces by using an inversely warped Z-buffer to clip volume rays against pre-rendered geometry. Unlike pure volume renderers, it allows for interactive classification and clipping modes (transparent or MIP) while maintaining geometric accuracy.

### [Perspective Shear-Warp](6047-perspective-shear-warp.md)
Perspective Shear-Warp is an object-order volume rendering algorithm that extends the parallel Shear-Warp method to handle perspective projections by applying a distance-dependent scale factor during the shear phase. It solves the problem of diverging viewing rays in perspective projection by ensuring that sampling remains uniform within each volume slice, thereby avoiding the complex multirate filtering required by naive ray-casting. Unlike parallel Shear-Warp, it is more computationally expensive due to the additional resampling and control flow complexity, but it remains efficient by maintaining scanline-based traversal and enabling early ray termination.

### [VolumePro 500 Implementation](8161-volumepro-500-implementation.md)
The VolumePro 500 is a hardware-accelerated volume rendering system based on the Cube-4 architecture, designed to render $256^3$ or smaller volumes at 30 frames per second. It distinguishes itself from software-based shear-warp implementations by offloading the core ray-casting loop, gradient estimation, and shading to dedicated silicon, achieving performance independent of data classification complexity. It builds on the [Shear-warp](24-shear-warp.md) factorization but replaces the standard resampling and compositing stages with a brute-force, axis-aligned processing pipeline optimized for memory coherence via 3D skewing.

### Back-to-front polygon rendering with display lists
Renders parallel polygons from back to front to satisfy linear alpha blending requirements for compositing [S8, unofficial]. The method defines six display lists (two directions along each of three axes). The renderer determines the largest absolute component of the view vector (x, y, or z) and its sign, then executes the corresponding display list [S8, unofficial]. A pitfall is that polygons are never viewed edge-on, limiting oblique viewing angles [S8, unofficial].

### Shear-Warp Factorization Rendered Examples Pipeline
The pipeline components include a gradient processor, matrix multiplication processor, shader, and classifier [S9, unofficial]. The process applies a rotation transformation matrix $M_{rot}$ with rotation angle $\alpha$ to the volume data, applies classification transfer functions to make soft tissues completely transparent (leaving only bone surfaces visible), and applies a Phong fast lighting model to shade the image [S9, unofficial].

### Coordinate System Conventions
A set of six distinct coordinate systems is used to track transformations in the shear-warp algorithm, each identified by a unique single character [S10, unofficial]. The systems are: 'o' (object space, actual volume data coordinates), 's' (standard object space, after permutation), 'd' (deformed space, 3D coordinates after shear), 'i' (intermediate image space, 2D coordinates within intermediate image), 'w' (world coordinate space), and 'v' (viewport space, 2D output window coordinates) [S10, unofficial]. Transition matrices between coordinate systems are named using the source and destination identifiers, e.g., $M_{ow}$ for object-to-world, and $M_{wo}$ for world-to-object [S10, unofficial].

### Parallel Shear-Warp on Shared Memory
A parallel volume rendering algorithm for shared-memory multiprocessors that minimizes computation, synchronization, and data communication time [S10, unofficial]. The algorithm is based on the shear-warp serial volume rendering algorithm to minimize computation time. It minimizes synchronization time by using dynamic load balancing and a task partition that minimizes synchronization events. It is implemented for shared-memory multiprocessors to leverage hardware support for low-latency fine-grain communication and hardware caching to hide latency [S10, unofficial]. A pitfall is that cache locality requirements impose a limit on parallelism; shared-memory machines with hundreds of processors are only useful for rendering very large data sets [S10, unofficial].

### Parallel Projection Rendering 3
Uses bilinear interpolation and backward projection convolution [S4, unofficial]. The method traverses 2 voxel scanlines simultaneously to produce one intermediate image scanline, which lies between the two voxel scanlines [S4, unofficial]. It uses a lookup table for shading and another lookup table to correct voxel opacity for view angle, accounting for apparent slice thickness dependence on angle [S4, unofficial]. After compositing, the 2D intermediate image is warped to the final image using a general purpose affine image warper with bilinear filter [S4, unofficial]. The run length encoded (RLE) data structure is created on the fly but is nearly view-independent; three encodings are created, one for each principal view direction, because transparent voxels are not stored, making the size tractable [S4, unofficial].

### Gaussian Volumetric Representation for Shear-Warp Visualization
A Gaussian-based volumetric representation proposed to address the high computational cost of large volumetric datasets while preserving anatomical fidelity and maintaining high rendering speeds in Shear-Warp visualization [S11, abstract only, unofficial].

### Warping Fields
A technique using a template RGB$\alpha$ volume $T(x)$ and a warp volume $W^{-1}(x)$ to alter effective voxel resolution and model motion, where $W^{-1}$ maps output positions to template sample locations [S12]. The final volume value is computed by first evaluating the value of the inverse warp $W^{-1}(x)$, then sampling the template volume $T$ at the resulting warped point [S12]. A pitfall is that forward warps cannot represent resolution-increasing transformations without additional memory; inverse warps map small output areas to larger template areas, allowing higher resolution details while remaining well-defined everywhere for usable gradients [S12].

## Background
The Shear-warp algorithm was designed by Lacroute et al. in 1994 [S2, unofficial][S12]. It was recognized as the fastest software render algorithm at the time [S2, unofficial][S12]. The basic idea is to factorize the projection matrix into a 3D shear and 2D warp [S1, unofficial]. Using the shearing, the data set is transformed into sheared object space where all viewing rays are parallel to one coordinate axis and the volume is considered as a stack of 2D 2D slices [S1, unofficial]. The intermediate image is then warped to the image plane [S1, unofficial].

The algorithm was implemented in VolumePro hardware, which was specialized for this algorithm [S2, unofficial][S12]. VolumePro was the first single-chip hardware compatible with consumer PCs for real-time volume rendering [S2, unofficial]. It was based on the Cube-4 framework by Pfister et al. [S2, unofficial]. Instead of linear interpolation, trilinear interpolation was performed to achieve better image quality [S2, unofficial]. Other features, such as super-sampling and cropping, were also incorporated into the VolumePro's architecture [S2, unofficial].

The algorithm assumes the view direction vector $v_o$ is mostly parallel to the +z axis ($v_{o,z} > v_{o,x}$ and $v_{o,z} > v_{o,y}$) to define shear slopes [S7, unofficial]. If the view is along x or y (or negative x or y), the voxel coordinates must be reordered by transposing the coordinate axes [S3, unofficial]. Artifacts may occur from the sampling as the viewpoint approaches a 45° angle from any axis [S3, unofficial][S6, book]. The Nyquist theorem is almost always violated due to varying sampling rate, leading to staircasing artifacts for diagonal views (e.g., at 45°) [S3, unofficial]. Blurring occurs for magnified views because the volume is pre-shaded [S3, unofficial]. If the opacity transfer function changes, the RLE volume must be re-encoded, making it not good for interactive iso-surface modification [S3, unofficial].
